dialog.resetBody: This clears the canvas. All elements and wires will be removed.
dialog.switchBody: This clears the canvas so you can start fresh at the new level.

file.menuHint: Save your chain, open one, or share it
file.saveBody: Your chain is saved as a file (usually in your Downloads folder). Open it again later with File → Open.
file.pictureTitle: Save a picture of your chain
file.pictureBody: A PNG picture of everything on the canvas — for a worksheet or a chat. The chain is hidden inside the picture too: File → Open turns it back into the chain.
file.downloadBody: The whole app in one file. Double-click it and it opens in your web browser — no internet, nothing to install. Copy it to a USB stick or a shared folder for a class; saved chains open in it too. For a newer version later, download it again. (This website also works offline once you have visited it: your browser keeps a copy.)
file.openBody: There are already elements on the canvas. Replace them with this chain, or add it beside them?
file.levelReplace: It was made at the {level} level: replacing the canvas switches the app to {level}.
file.levelAdd: It was made at the {level} level, so the app switches to {level}.
file.skipped: {count} elements were left out: this version of the app does not have them.
file.linkCopied: Link copied. Anyone who opens it gets a copy of this chain.
file.linkLong: Link copied — but it is very long, so some chat apps may cut it short. Saving a file is safer.
file.linkFailed: The link could not be copied. Save the chain to a file instead.
file.linkBroken: This link is broken or cut short, so the chain could not be opened. Ask for the link again.
file.pictureSaved: Picture saved — usually in your Downloads folder.
file.pictureFailed: The picture could not be made. Try again, or save a file instead.
file.notChain: This file isn't a saved signal chain. Open a .json file or a picture saved from this app.
file.noChainInPicture: This picture has no chain inside. Only pictures saved from this app can be opened.

toolbar.snapHint: Line elements up on the dotted grid

tools.label: What a click does
tools.dragHint: Drag an element to move it. Drag empty space to look around the canvas.
tools.selectHint: Click elements to pick several (click again to drop one), or drag a box around them. Then right-click one to copy or duplicate them all.
tools.removeHint: Click an element or a wire to remove it.
tools.redoHint: Bring back the change you just took back.

connecting.hint: Click a highlighted input. Click empty space to add a bend.

beginner.title: Beginner
beginner.description: Simple chain: microphone → preamp → EQ → compressor → speaker.

intermediate.title: Intermediate
intermediate.description: Full chain including channel fader and master bus.

advanced.title: Advanced
advanced.description: Full chain with all processing stages.

meters.tipBeginner: How strong the signal is: the taller the bar, the louder. Blue: too quiet. Green: good. Yellow: getting hot. Red: it distorts.
meters.tip: A meter like a recording program's. The solid bar is the average over the last 0.3 seconds — how loud it sounds. The light bar shows the peaks, the loudest moments, falling back slowly. The mark is the loudest peak of the last 3 seconds. The grey fog at the bottom is the noise you hear when the music stops. The number under it is the average over the whole 10 seconds of sound.

curve.tip: Left to right: the level coming in. Bottom to top: the level going out. On the dashed diagonal nothing changes; where the curve leaves it, this card is at work. The Peaks and Average marks move with the sound as it plays; the Noise mark shows what comes out when the music stops. A faint mark on the diagonal shows where a mark would be without the card. A Peaks mark above the curve: the start of a note got through before the card reacted (its Attack).

warnings.domainMixedBus: Cannot mix analog and digital signals — insert a DAC before this bus, or keep signals in the same domain.
warnings.digitalToAmp: Amp cannot amplify a digital signal. Insert a DAC before the amp to convert back to analog.
warnings.digitalToSpeaker: Speaker cannot receive a digital signal. Insert a DAC before the speaker.
warnings.adcExpectsAnalog: ADC expects an analog input. Connect it after analog gear, not after another ADC or digital node.
warnings.dacExpectsDigital: DAC expects a digital input. Connect it after an ADC or other digital node.

hum.tip: A hum from the DI Box's ground loop rides along with the signal, like any noise: a boost lifts it with the music, a fader turns both down together — the gap between them stays. Only Ground Lift on the DI Box takes it away.

tips.peaks: The average is how loud it sounds; the peaks are its loudest moments — what clips first. On a meter, the solid bar is the average, the light bar and the thin line beyond it the peaks. A voice peaks about 12 dB above its average, drums about 18. A compressor brings them closer; clipping cuts them off.
tips.room: How far the loudest moments are below the clip level (+20 dBu, or 0 dBFS after an ADC), where every stage distorts. Engineers call this room headroom. {careful} dB or less: careful, a louder note will distort.
tips.hiss: Every powered device adds a little hiss. This is how far it sits below the music — engineers call it the signal-to-noise ratio: {audible} dB or more and you won't notice it; less, and you hear it in the quiet moments. Make the gain early, at the Preamp: turning up later lifts the hiss too. The grey fog on the meter is the noise.

readings.hissHereTip: From this element on, the hiss is less than {audible} dB below the music, so you hear it in the quiet moments. Usually the signal reaching it is too weak: turn up early (the Preamp) instead of later.
readings.notConnectedTip: Nothing is plugged into its output yet. Wire it to another element: then it plays, and its readings show.

eq.label: Parametric Equalizer
eq.widthShelf: A shelf has no width — turn Shelf off to use it
eq.shelfHint: Shelf: raise or lower everything past this frequency evenly, instead of a hump around it
eq.graphHint: Drag a coloured dot up to make that range louder, down to make it quieter, or sideways to move it to lower or higher sounds. Double-click a dot to set it back to 0 dB (no change).
eq.graphHintWidth: Scroll over a dot to make its band wider or narrower.

graphic-eq.label: Graphic EQ
graphic-eq.hint: Drag a slider up to boost that frequency, down to cut it. Double-click = 0 dB.
graphic-eq.flatHint: Set every slider back to 0 dB

speaker.label: Speaker / Monitor
speaker.needsAmp: Silent — needs an Amplifier before it

active-speaker.label: Active Speaker
active-speaker.blown: Blown! An amplifier's output is far too strong for it.

headphones.label: Headphones
headphones.blown: Blown! An amplifier's output is far too strong for them.

di-box.label: DI Box
di-box.description: Turns a guitar or keyboard into a mic-level signal the desk can take: no high notes lost, no noise on a long cable.
di-box.micLevel: mic level · to the desk's Preamp
di-box.instrumentLevel: instrument level · to a guitar amp
di-box.hum: Hum! The guitar amp and the desk are both grounded through this box. Turn Ground Lift on.

instrument.needsDi: No DI Box: the high notes get lost

hints.sine: Sine: a steady test tone. Its loudest moments are only 3 dB above its average — it is the last to clip.
hints.noise: Noise: hiss across every pitch. Its loudest moments are about 12 dB above its average, like a voice.
hints.click: Click: short pulses, like a metronome. Each one jumps about 18 dB above the average — at the same level, these clip first.

pan.label: Pan
pan.direction: Where you will hear it: between the left (L) and the right (R) speaker.

matrix-bus.label: Matrix Bus
matrix-bus.empty: Plug in a mix: an output of a Master Bus or an Aux Bus
matrix-bus.sendHint: How much of this bus goes in. Point here to light up where it comes from.

balance.label: Balance
balance.direction: Which side is louder: turning towards one side fades the other.

nodeControls.turnOff: On — click to bypass it (the signal then passes through unchanged)
nodeControls.turnOn: Bypassed — the signal passes through unchanged. Click to turn it back on

nodeMenu.bypass: Bypass — let the signal pass through unchanged
nodeMenu.duplicateLeft: Put a copy on the left
nodeMenu.duplicateRight: Put a copy on the right

stereo.toggleHint: Mono = one channel. Stereo = Left and Right travel together on one wire (drawn as a double line).

hints.speech: Speech: someone talking, with pauses between the sentences. The loudest moments are about 12 dB above the average.
hints.singing: Singing: a voice holding notes. The loudest moments are about 12 dB above the average.
hints.music: Music: keys, a bass and a shaker playing a song. The loudest moments are about 12 dB above the average.
hints.drums: Drums: sharp hits jump about 18 dB above the average — at the same level, they reach the clip level sooner.

ports.send: Matrix send (L + R, after the fader)

di-box.out: XLR Out — mic level, to the desk
di-box.direct: Direct Out — the guitar as it is, to a guitar amp

guitar-amp.in: Guitar in — from an Instrument or a DI Box's Direct Out
guitar-amp.sound: Sound — put a Microphone in front of it

mic.in: Sound in — the Guitar Amp this microphone is in front of

relay.in-a: PRE — wire in the signal from before the fader
relay.in-b: POST — wire in the signal from after the fader

unplugMenu.title: Wires on this input
unplugMenu.hint: Point at a wire to light up its chain

palette.rightClickTip: Tip: right-click an element on the canvas for help, to bypass it or to remove it.
palette.hide: Hide the elements panel (more room for the canvas)

mic.what: The microphone converts sound (acoustic energy) into an electrical signal. It outputs a very weak voltage — typically around -60 dBu for a dynamic microphone.
mic.why: Everything starts here. The quality and placement of the microphone determines the raw material for the entire signal chain. A good source signal makes everything downstream easier.
mic.tip: Its wire is blue (too quiet) — that is completely normal and expected at this stage. The preamp's job is to fix that. Put it in front of a Guitar Amp (wire the amp's Sound into it) and it picks up the amp: the louder the amp plays, the louder the microphone. From Intermediate on, choose what it picks up: Speech, Singing or Drums. Drum hits jump much further above the average, so they reach the clip level sooner.
mic.readings: The Hiss reading starts at 66 dB below the signal: the quiet hiss of the room and of the microphone itself. Engineers call it the noise floor — the cleanest this signal will ever be. Every powered card after it adds a little hiss of its own, so on the way to the speakers this gap can only shrink (a Noise Gate can hide it in the pauses); your job is to keep it big. The Peaks reading says 12 dB for a voice, speaking or singing, and 18 for Drums.

line-in.what: A line input accepts signals that are already at "line level" — roughly -10 dBu for consumer gear, +4 dBu for professional gear. This is the standard level used between devices: from a keyboard, audio interface, or effects unit into a mixer.
line-in.why: Line-level signals are strong enough to drive mixing and processing gear directly without a preamp. They sit well above the noise floor and well below the clipping point.
line-in.tip: If your line-level signal looks green (-40 to 0 dBu) you are good to go. If it is too quiet, the source device may have its own output level control — adjust that first before adding gain in the chain. Set it to Stereo for a source that has a left and a right side, like a keyboard or a phone — both travel on one wire. From Intermediate on, choose what it plays: Music (a song) or Drums (a drum machine). Drum hits jump much further above the average, so they reach the clip level sooner.
line-in.readings: The Hiss reading starts at 80 dB below the signal: a line source is very clean, and it needs no Preamp to reach a healthy level. Switch to Drums and the Peaks reading goes from 12 to 18 dB above the average: Room before clipping shrinks by those 6 dB, while the meter's bar does not move.

instrument.what: An electric guitar, bass or keyboard. Its signal is stronger than a microphone's (about −30 dBu) but still well below line level.
instrument.why: It only sounds right into the right kind of input: a guitar amp, or a DI Box. Plugged straight into a desk input, the high notes get lost and a long cable picks up noise — the card warns you when that happens.
instrument.tip: Two ways to the audience: Instrument → DI Box → Preamp, or Instrument → Guitar Amp with a Microphone in front of it. Many engineers do both at once, feeding the amp from the DI Box's Direct Out.
instrument.readings: The Peaks reading says 15 dB above the average: each pluck jumps out above the ringing note. The Hiss reading starts at 70 dB below the signal — the pickups and the cable.

gain.what: A gain stage turns a signal up or down by a set amount: right of 0 dB makes it louder, left of 0 dB quieter, and all the way left switches it off. Placed right after a microphone, this same card becomes a Preamp.
gain.why: Every device in a chain expects a certain level. A gain stage fixes a signal that arrives too weak or too strong — a quiet line source, say, or a hot one before an effect that would clip.
gain.tip: Start at 0 dB (no change) and move it only until the meter after it sits in the green (−40 to 0 dBu). Turning up raises the noise along with the signal; turning down too far leaves the next stage too little to work with.
gain.readings: A gain stage moves the music and the hiss that came with it by the same amount, so the Hiss reading stays about the same — only this card's own little hiss is added. If it drops a lot here and the card gets the tag “You can hear hiss here”, the signal arriving was too weak for this card's own hiss: make the gain earlier, at the Preamp, instead.

preamp.what: The preamplifier (preamp) boosts a weak mic-level signal up to "line level" — strong enough for the rest of the chain to work with. Typical gain: +20 to +60 dB. It is what the Gain card becomes when you place it right after a microphone, or after a DI Box's XLR Out.
preamp.why: Without enough gain here, all downstream processors — EQ, compressor, fader — work with a weak signal and introduce more noise. Too much gain causes distortion before anything else can help.
preamp.tip: Aim for the output to land well inside the green zone — about −20 to −10 dBu for a voice. This is called gain staging, and it starts right here at the preamp. At the bottom of the green (−40 dBu) the signal is so weak that the hiss of the devices after it can be heard; turn up much further and the loudest moments come close to clipping.
preamp.readings: Follow the Hiss reading card by card to the speaker: with the Preamp at +50 dB it stays clean all the way (50 dB or more). Now try the classic mistake: the Preamp at +20, made up later with a Gain or the Fader. The level at the end is the same, but the hiss ends 40 dB or less below the music, and the card after the Preamp says “You can hear hiss here”: its own hiss landed on a signal 30 dB too weak. That is why gain is made early, at the Preamp — as long as Room before clipping stays above 6 dB.

hpf.what: The High-Pass Filter (HPF) removes frequencies below a chosen cutoff point. Everything below that frequency is rolled off — "blocked". Everything above it "passes" through unchanged.
hpf.why: Microphones and instruments pick up low-frequency rumble: air conditioning, footsteps, handling noise, mic stand vibration. These frequencies serve no musical purpose and just muddy the mix. The HPF cleans them up before they reach the EQ or compressor.
hpf.tip: For most vocals start at 80–120 Hz. For acoustic guitar, try 100–150 Hz. Never use HPF on a kick drum or bass — you'll cut the fundamental frequency you actually want. The curve display shows exactly which frequencies you're removing.
hpf.readings: Like every powered card it adds a little hiss of its own before it works — far below a healthy signal, so the Hiss reading barely moves. If this card gets the tag “You can hear hiss here”, the signal reaching it is too weak: turn up the Preamp before it.

eq.what: The equalizer (EQ) shapes the tonal character of the signal by boosting or cutting frequency ranges. Each band targets a frequency area: Low (body), Mid (presence), High (air and clarity). A Bell band makes a peak or dip around its frequency; a Shelf band boosts or cuts everything below or above it, evenly.
eq.why: Every sound source has frequencies that help or hurt its purpose. A vocal may need less boxiness around 400 Hz, more presence at 3 kHz, and more air at 10 kHz. The EQ lets you sculpt that precisely.
eq.tip: EQ is mostly subtractive in professional practice — cut what you don't need rather than boosting everything. Boosting adds energy; cutting cleans up the mix. In Intermediate the Equalizer has three knobs like a simple mixing desk: Low and High are shelves, Mid is a bell. "Parametric" means you set each band's frequency and width yourself — that is what the Parametric Equalizer in Advanced adds, with a curve you can drag and a Bell / Shelf choice for Low and High. Feed it a stereo wire and both sides get the same settings.
eq.readings: Like every powered card, it adds a little hiss of its own (−80 dBu) before it works. Next to a healthy signal that is far below, and the Hiss reading barely moves; after a Preamp set 30 dB too low it is audible, and this card gets the tag “You can hear hiss here”. Turn up the Preamp, not the EQ: a boost lifts the hiss with the music.

graphic-eq.what: The Graphic EQ divides the spectrum into fixed frequency bands (here: 31 bands, three per octave — a third of an octave each — from 20 Hz to 20 kHz). Each band has its own fader — push it up to boost that band, pull it down to cut. The line across the sliders shows the shape you have drawn. Wire it to the L or R of a bus or its Main Fader (or feed it any stereo wire) and it works on both sides: the whole mix comes in on one wire and leaves as L and R, ready for an amplifier or two speakers. The sliders then split in two — Left on top, Right below — so each side can be shaped on its own; the right side starts as a copy of the left. Fed one channel, it stays single-channel.
graphic-eq.why: Graphic EQs are found on the master output of PA systems as the final tool for correcting room acoustics — a sudden peak at 4 kHz, a resonant boom at 63 Hz. They are less precise than parametric EQs but faster to use for broad shaping.
graphic-eq.tip: In live sound the graphic EQ on the master output is used mainly to prevent feedback and correct for the room, not to shape the mix. Keep moves gentle — small cuts (−3 to −6 dB) solve most problems. Large boosts cause feedback and distortion.

comp.what: The compressor reduces the dynamic range of the signal — it automatically turns down loud peaks and can be used with makeup gain to raise the overall level. It makes quiet parts relatively louder and loud parts relatively quieter.
comp.why: Live performances and recordings have wide dynamic ranges. Without compression, loud notes clip and quiet notes get lost. Compression makes the signal more consistent and controlled.
comp.tip: Watch the curve: its marks show what comes out over a few seconds of the sound. The compressor turns the loud moments down, so the Average comes down by about its gain reduction. Attack decides what happens to the Peaks: a slower Attack lets the start of each note or word through before it reacts — the Peaks mark sits above the curve and the peaks end up further from the average (engineers keep that "punch" on drums). A quick Attack (1–5 ms) catches more of it; on a sound whose notes start softly, like singing, the peaks then come closer to the average. A compressor evens out how loud the music is — to stop its loudest moments, put a Limiter after it. Release is how quickly it lets go after a loud moment. The Noise stays under the Threshold and is not turned down, so the hiss comes closer to the music by as much as the compressor turns the average down; makeup gain then lifts all three together. 2–6 dB of gain reduction is transparent and musical. More than 10 dB starts to sound pumped and squashed — which can be an effect in itself. When a stereo wire comes in, both sides are turned down together (linked) — the louder side decides — so the sound does not drift left or right.
comp.readings: The Average comes down here by the gain reduction. Watch the Peaks reading: on a speaking voice the start of each word gets through before the Attack (10 ms) acts, so the peaks hardly come down — about 12 dB above the average going in, 17 coming out. At 1 ms it catches a little more (16). Switch the Microphone to Singing: its notes start softly, and with a 1 ms Attack the peaks come closer to the average (10). The Hiss reading shrinks by as much as the average is turned down (the gain-reduction meter).

fader.what: The channel fader controls the volume of this signal as it enters the mix. Unity gain (0 dB) means the signal passes through unchanged. Moving it down attenuates the signal.
fader.why: Every instrument in a mix needs to sit at the right level relative to everything else. The fader is how you set that balance. It is the primary mixing control.
fader.tip: In a mix, most faders end up below unity. The art of mixing is in the relative balance between all channels, not in making each one as loud as possible. Fed a stereo wire, one fader moves both sides together.
fader.readings: Pulling the fader down turns the music and its hiss down together: the Hiss reading stays about the same, and Room before clipping grows. Pushing it above 0 dB to rescue a weak channel lifts the hiss too — if the fader gets the tag “You can hear hiss here”, the Preamp is set too low.

main-fader.what: A fader wired straight after a bus becomes its Main Fader. It controls the whole mix with one handle — left and right move together — and the bus's L and R outputs move onto it, so the speakers now hang off the fader. Its Matrix send moves too, so Matrix Buses always get the mix after this fader.
main-fader.why: This is the last level control before the speakers: it turns the whole mix up or down without changing the balance you built on the channels. One handle means left and right can never drift apart.
main-fader.tip: Take a second wire from the bus's Mix output: it does not change when you move this fader, because it leaves before the fader. That is where a pre-fade listen (PFL) path starts. Effects such as a limiter may sit between the bus and this fader — it stays the Main Fader.
main-fader.readings: It moves the whole mix and its hiss together: the Hiss reading stays about the same, Room before clipping changes. But if the bus before it already reads “it distorts”, this fader cannot fix it — the peaks were cut off on the bus, and turning down afterwards does not bring them back (the Peaks reading stays smaller). Turn the channels down instead.

amp.what: A power amplifier takes a line-level signal and boosts it to speaker-driving level — adding significant current, not just voltage. A passive speaker (one without a built-in amp) requires a power amplifier to produce any sound. Its Volume knob only turns down: at 0 dB (fully up) the signal goes on unchanged, which is already plenty for the speaker. Turning it up further would only make a good line-level signal clip. Wire it to the L or R of a bus, its Main Fader or a Graphic EQ (or feed it any stereo wire) and it becomes a two-channel amp: the whole mix comes in on one wire, channel A takes the left side and channel B the right, each with its own Volume knob and its own output, L and R — one per speaker. Fed one channel, it stays a single-channel amp.
amp.why: Line-level signals are powerful enough for mixing and processing, but not powerful enough to physically move a speaker cone. The power amp provides the current needed to do the work.
amp.tip: Power amps are rated in watts. For studio monitors you typically need 50–100 W. For live PA systems, 500–2000 W per side is common. More wattage = more headroom before clipping, not necessarily more loudness.

switch.what: A switch (or mute button) is the simplest control in a signal chain. When it is on, the signal passes through unchanged. When it is off, the signal is completely cut — silence.
switch.why: Muting is used to silence a channel between takes, to prevent feedback when a microphone is not in use, or to isolate a track during a mix.
switch.tip: In live sound, muting microphones when not in use prevents bleed, handling noise, and feedback. It is a habit every sound engineer develops quickly.

aux-bus.what: An aux bus collects several signals and adds them together. Its one input takes as many wires as you like. In Mono everything leaves on one wire. Switch it to Stereo to keep left and right apart: the mix then leaves on two wires, L and R. In Stereo, a Fader wired to L or R becomes its Main Fader, just like on the Master Bus.
aux-bus.why: Use it to group sources that belong together — all backing vocals, all drums — so one control sets their combined level, or to send a separate mix to a monitor or an effect.
aux-bus.tip: Try this: set a Line Input to Stereo and wire it into a Mono aux bus. Left and right are added together and the level jumps by about 6 dB. That is why a stereo mix can suddenly get louder (or clip) when it is folded down to mono.

matrix-bus.what: A matrix bus is a mix of your mixes. Only finished mixes go in, after their fader — the Master Bus or an Aux Bus — never a single microphone or instrument. Wire a bus's L or R output into the matrix and the wire becomes its Matrix send: one stereo wire that carries left and right together, drawn as a twin line in its own colour and marked L+R. A mono Aux Bus goes in from its output, or from the Fader after it, and lands on both sides at the same level. Each bus gets one knob on the card that sets how much of it goes in. A matrix bus is always stereo: its mix leaves on two wires, L and R.
matrix-bus.why: Different places need a different blend, and the main mix must not change for them: small speakers along the front edge of the stage that need more vocals, delay speakers at the back of a hall, a speaker in the lobby, a feed for a recording or a livestream. Put a Fader after it to set its overall level — that Fader becomes its Main Fader.
matrix-bus.tip: Try this: give the Master Bus a Main Fader, then wire the fader's L output into the matrix. Move the Main Fader: the matrix follows, because the send leaves after the fader — that is how matrix sends work on a real mixing desk. Try a microphone too: the matrix input does not light up, because a microphone is not a mix.

balance.what: A balance control adjusts the relative loudness between the Left and Right channels of a stereo signal. At centre, both channels pass through equally. Turning left fades out the right channel; turning right fades out the left channel.
balance.why: Useful when a stereo source sounds off-centre — for example, a recording where the guitarist is too far left — nudge the balance to compensate without re-mixing the source.
balance.tip: Balance is what the Pan card becomes when you feed it a stereo wire. At centre both sides pass at full level — no −3 dB like a pan knob. Turning it left only fades the right side; the left side never gets louder. Keep it near centre unless a stereo source really sounds off-centre.

master-bus.what: The master bus is the final mixing point where every channel is added together before the sound leaves the system. Its one input takes as many wires as you like; the mix leaves on two wires, L and R — one for each speaker. A stereo wire keeps its left and right. A wire from another bus's L or R output stays on its side. A mono wire lands on both sides at full level — put a Pan knob in front to place it. Wire a Fader to its L or R output and it becomes the Main Fader: the L and R outputs move onto the fader.
master-bus.why: The master bus controls the overall output level. It is also the place for final mix bus processing — subtle compression or limiting to control peaks and add cohesion.
master-bus.tip: Leave headroom on the master bus — keep it in the green, at or below 0 dBu (unity). Above that it turns yellow (hot): less room is left before its loudest moments reach +20 dBu and clip, and a limiter or the next device has less to work with.
master-bus.readings: Every wire you add makes the mix louder — two identical signals read 6 dB more — so Room before clipping shrinks with every channel. At 0 the loudest moments of the whole mix are cut off (“it distorts”), and nothing after the bus brings them back. Keep it above 6 dB: when it gets close, bring the channel faders down together.

speaker.what: A passive speaker converts electrical signal back into sound, but it has no built-in amplifier. It needs a separate power amplifier (Amp node) to drive it — connecting one directly to line level will produce no sound.
speaker.why: Passive speakers are the standard in live sound PA systems and hi-fi setups. The amplifier is a separate unit chosen for its power output and impedance matching to the speaker.
speaker.tip: Connect an Amp node before this speaker. The amplifier provides the current needed to physically move the speaker cone. Without it, the signal is there but nothing moves.
speaker.readings: These readings are what the audience hears. The Hiss reading here is the signal-to-noise ratio of your whole chain: well set, 50 to 60 dB (clean); with the Preamp too low and made up later, 40 or less (you can hear it). Room before clipping at 0 means the speaker plays the distortion.

active-speaker.what: An active (powered) speaker has a built-in amplifier. It accepts line-level signals directly from a mixer, audio interface, or any line-level output — no separate power amp needed.
active-speaker.why: Active speakers are the standard in modern studio monitors and portable PA setups. The built-in amplifier is matched to the speaker driver, which is why powered monitors tend to have more consistent, accurate sound.
active-speaker.tip: The volume knob adjusts the final output level. Good gain staging means getting a healthy green signal to this speaker — then use the volume knob to set how loud you want to listen, not to compensate for a too-quiet or too-loud chain. Never plug it into an Amplifier's output: that signal is already strong enough to drive a passive speaker, far too much for the line input of a speaker with its own amp inside — it blows.
active-speaker.readings: These readings are what the audience hears. The Hiss reading here is the signal-to-noise ratio of your whole chain: well set, 50 to 60 dB (clean); with the Preamp too low and made up later, 40 or less (you can hear it). The Volume knob moves the music and the hiss together — it cannot clean up a noisy chain.

headphones.what: Headphones let one person listen to the chain: the engineer checking a channel, or a musician hearing their monitor mix. Here they work like an Active Speaker — a line-level signal in, a Volume knob for how loud.
headphones.why: In a studio or on stage not everyone can listen on the speakers. Headphones put the sound right at one person's ears, without the room around it.
headphones.tip: Like an Active Speaker, never plug them into an Amplifier's output: a power amp's signal is meant for a passive speaker and is far too strong for them — they blow.
headphones.readings: What reaches them is what that listener hears: the same Hiss and Room before clipping as the card before. The Volume knob moves the music and the hiss together.

di-box.what: A DI box (Direct Injection) takes a guitar, bass or keyboard and turns it into a mic-level signal for the desk: its XLR Out is about 20 dB quieter than what goes in, so a Gain after it works as a Preamp, just like after a microphone. Its Direct Out passes the instrument on unchanged, for a guitar amp on stage.
di-box.why: Plugged straight into a desk input, a guitar loses its high notes and its long cable picks up noise. The DI box gives the instrument the input it needs and sends a strong, clean signal down the long cable to the desk.
di-box.tip: Wire Direct Out to a Guitar Amp and XLR Out to the desk at the same time and you may get a hum: both are plugged into the mains, and their grounds meet through the box. Turn Ground Lift on to break that loop — the hum goes away.

guitar-amp.what: A guitar amplifier with its own speaker: it takes a guitar straight in and plays it out loud on stage. Its sound is what a microphone in front of it picks up.
guitar-amp.why: Guitarists shape much of their sound with their amp. To get it to the audience, put a Microphone in front of it (a dotted line: sound through the air, not a cable) and send the microphone to a Preamp like any other.
guitar-amp.tip: Feed it from an Instrument, or from a DI Box's Direct Out to send the same guitar to the desk as well. Turn its Volume down and the microphone in front of it gets quieter too.

generator.what: A signal generator makes a test sound by itself: a steady tone (Sine), hiss (Noise) or short pulses (Click). Its Level knob sets how strong it is — 0 dBu is the level the desk is built around. Switch it to Stereo to test a stereo chain: the same sound on Left and Right, on one wire.
generator.why: Engineers send a known sound through a chain to check every stage before the musicians arrive. Every sound has loudest moments (its peaks) above its average level, and the gap depends on the sound: about 3 dB for a sine, 18 dB for clicks. The meters show the average; the peaks are what clip.
generator.tip: Try this: set Sine at +10 dBu — its wire is yellow (hot). Switch to Click at the same level and the wire turns red: the clicks' peaks reach the clip level (+20 dBu) while their average has not moved.
generator.readings: At the same Level the Peaks reading depends on the sound: Sine 3 dB above the average, Noise 12, Click 18 — so at 0 dBu Room before clipping reads 17, 8 and 2 dB (careful). Its own hiss is 90 dB below the signal, cleaner than any instrument: any hiss you see further along was added by the chain.

noise-gate.what: A noise gate is a switch controlled by level. When the signal rises above the threshold, the gate opens and the signal passes through unchanged. When the signal falls below the threshold, the gate closes and the output is silence.
noise-gate.why: Every microphone and cable picks up some background noise — air conditioning hum, electrical interference, room ambience. Between musical phrases, when the performer is quiet, that noise is audible. The gate simply closes during those quiet moments, removing the noise before it reaches the mix.
noise-gate.tip: Set the threshold between the noise and the quietest part of the signal: on the curve, put the dashed Threshold line between the Noise dot and the Average dot. The Noise dot then drops to the bottom — the gate closes in the pauses — while the music passes untouched. Too high, and the Average drops too: the gate cuts into the music and chops off the start of notes. Too low, and the noise gets through. OPEN / CLOSED shows what the gate is doing to the music right now. Range is how far it turns down when closed: all the way (−80 dB, silence) or only a little, so the background drops without vanishing. Attack is how fast it opens, Hold keeps it open for a moment after the sound stops, and Release is how gently it closes.
noise-gate.readings: Set well, the gate shuts the hiss off in the pauses: the Hiss reading jumps far up (clean), while the Peaks reading and Room before clipping stay as they were. If those change too, the gate is cutting into the music.

limiter.what: A limiter is a compressor with an extremely high ratio — effectively infinite. It sets a hard ceiling: no signal can exceed the threshold, no matter how loud the input gets. Below the ceiling, the signal passes through unchanged. Wire it to the L or R of a bus (or of its Main Fader) and it takes the whole mix: one stereo wire in, L and R out — and a Fader after it is the Main Fader.
limiter.why: Limiters protect equipment and listeners from sudden loud peaks. A drum hit, a mic bump, a loud vocal phrase — without limiting, any of these can clip the mix bus, damage amplifiers, or cause hearing damage at high volumes. The limiter is the safety net at the end of the chain.
limiter.tip: Unlike a compressor, a limiter is meant to be invisible — you should not hear it working. If you see the 'Limiting' indicator light up often, the signal going into the limiter is too hot. Fix it earlier in the chain rather than relying on the limiter to tame a consistently loud signal. On the curve, the Peaks stop at the Ceiling; the Average comes down a little with them (each caught peak turns that moment down), and the Noise below passes untouched. If the Average comes down a lot, the limiter is working far too hard.
limiter.readings: Once it works, the peaks stop at the Ceiling: the Peaks reading gets smaller and Room before clipping stops shrinking, however hot the input gets. Each caught peak turns that moment down, so the Average drops a little too. If the Peaks reading is much smaller here than on the card before, the limiter is working too hard — turn down earlier in the chain.

pad.what: A pad is a fixed attenuator — a passive circuit that drops the signal level by a set amount, usually 20 dB. It sits inline in the signal path. When the pad is engaged (button shows −20 dB), the signal is reduced by 20 dB. When disengaged, the signal passes through unchanged.
pad.why: Microphones in front of loud sources — kick drums, guitar amps, brass instruments — can produce a signal so strong that even the preamp at its lowest gain setting is too loud. The pad solves this by cutting the level before it even reaches the preamp's gain stage, preventing distortion at the input.
pad.tip: Engage the pad before you record if your input meter is clipping even with the gain turned all the way down. The 20 dB drop is a lot — if the signal then becomes too quiet, raise the preamp gain to compensate and find the right balance.
pad.readings: A pad adds no hiss of its own, but it turns the music and its noise down by 20 dB, so the Preamp after it adds its own hiss to a much weaker signal: on a microphone the Hiss reading after the Preamp drops from 64 to 48 dB. Use the pad only when the Preamp clips even at its lowest gain.

deesser.what: A de-esser is a frequency-selective compressor. It listens for harsh sibilance — the sharp hissing sounds of letters like 'S', 'SH', and 'CH' in vocal recordings — and automatically reduces only those frequencies when they get too loud. You set the frequency and threshold; the de-esser does the rest automatically.
deesser.why: Microphones and certain processing (especially EQ boosts in the 5–10 kHz range) can exaggerate sibilance until it becomes painful to listen to. A broadband compressor would make everything quieter, which is not the goal. The de-esser targets only the problem frequencies, leaving the rest of the voice untouched.
deesser.tip: Set the frequency to where the sibilance is worst — usually 5–8 kHz for most voices, sometimes up to 10 kHz for brighter voices. The gain reduction meter shows how much de-essing is happening. A little (1–3 dB) is transparent. Heavy de-essing (6+ dB) can make voices sound lispy.
deesser.readings: The Average and the Peaks hardly move here: only the “s” sounds come down, and the gain-reduction meter shows how far. On a speaking voice the starting threshold takes them down about 6 dB; switch the Microphone to Singing, with hardly any “s”, and it has almost nothing to do.

relay.what: A relay switch: two inputs, one output. Press a button and the signal comes from that input; the other one is cut off.
relay.why: It picks the point a signal is taken from with one press, without re-wiring: before or after a fader (PRE / POST), or before or after a group of elements — so it can skip several of them at once.
relay.tip: PRE is the top input, POST the one below; the chosen button is lit green. To skip elements, wire the signal from before them into one input and their output into the other.

pan.what: Feed it a mono signal and this is a Pan knob: it spreads that one signal between Left and Right and sends both out on one stereo wire. Fully left, only the left side gets it; fully right, only the right side. At centre each side gets it 3 dB quieter, so the overall loudness stays the same. Feed it a stereo wire and it turns into a Balance knob on its own.
pan.why: A mono signal — one microphone, one guitar — has no left or right of its own. Wired straight into a stereo bus it lands on both sides at full level: stuck in the middle and 3 dB louder than a centred pan. The Pan knob is how you place it anywhere between the speakers.
pan.tip: Compare: Line Input → Pan at centre → the Master shows 3 dB less on each side than the same Line Input wired straight into the Master. Then set the Line Input to Stereo: the card turns into Balance. A balance knob does not spread one signal, it only turns down one side of a signal that already has two.

adc.what: An Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) samples the continuously varying analog voltage from your gear thousands of times per second and converts each measurement into a digital number. The level scale changes from dBu (analog) to dBFS (digital full scale). With the standard alignment, 0 dBu (unity) becomes −18 dBFS — so the digital ceiling, 0 dBFS, is +18 dBu. Healthy analog levels land well below it.
adc.why: Computers work with numbers, not voltages. The ADC is the bridge between the physical world of microphones and amplifiers and the digital world of DAWs and plugins. Everything after the ADC is math, not electricity.
adc.tip: 0 dBFS is the ceiling in digital audio — there is no louder. Unlike analog gear which can go a few dB over nominal before distorting, digital clips instantly and harshly at 0 dBFS. Aim to keep peaks well below 0 dBFS (−18 to −6 dBFS) to protect against sudden transients.
adc.readings: From here on Room before clipping counts up to 0 dBFS, the digital ceiling (+18 dBu at the standard alignment), so the same signal reads 2 dB less room than before the converter. Cards working digitally after it add no hiss of their own: the Hiss reading travels on as it was.

dac.what: A Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) does the reverse of an ADC: it reads the digital numbers from your computer and reconstructs a continuously varying analog voltage. Using the same alignment, −18 dBFS becomes 0 dBu (unity) again, and anything after the DAC is back in the analog world.
dac.why: Speakers and amplifiers are analog devices — they respond to voltage, not numbers. The DAC converts the digital mix back into real electrical signal so you can hear it through speakers. Without a DAC, digital audio stays in the computer.
dac.tip: Place the DAC before any analog gear that follows — amplifiers, passive speakers, analog signal processors. The domain indicator on the node turns green (analog) after the DAC, confirming that everything downstream is back in the correct electrical domain.
